subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Models of development (cognitive, social, moral, language)
Development of the self (attachment, enculturation, peer influence, childhood experiences)

questions.q: In Piaget's theory, object permanence typically develops during the:
questions.explain: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor stage of infancy.

questions.q: Piaget's four stages, in order, are sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and:
questions.explain: The formal operational stage involves abstract, logical reasoning.

questions.q: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a child can do:
options: Alone and with guidance from a more knowledgeable other
questions.explain: Learning occurs in the ZPD with appropriate scaffolding from a more knowledgeable other.

questions.q: Adjusting support to a child's level and reducing it as they improve is called:
questions.explain: Scaffolding is tailored support within the ZPD, withdrawn as competence grows.

questions.q: Kohlberg's theory describes stages of:
questions.explain: Kohlberg proposed pre-conventional, conventional and post-conventional moral reasoning.

questions.q: A nativist view of language development (e.g. Chomsky) emphasises:
options: An innate capacity for language plus a sensitive period
Pure imitation with no innate basis
That language has no biological basis
questions.explain: Nativist accounts stress an innate language faculty and a sensitive period for acquisition.

questions.q: A teacher gives just enough hints for a pupil to solve a task slightly beyond their solo ability, then withdraws help. This illustrates:
options: Scaffolding within the zone of proximal development
questions.explain: Guided, fading support for a task just beyond independent ability is scaffolding within the ZPD.

questions.q: A contrast between Piaget and Vygotsky is that Vygotsky stressed:
options: The role of culture and social interaction in development
That stages do not exist at all
questions.explain: Vygotsky emphasised socially and culturally mediated learning, versus Piaget's lone-scientist child.

questions.q: In Piaget's theory, understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in appearance is called:
questions.explain: Conservation develops in the concrete operational stage.

questions.q: A 4-year-old thinks a tall thin glass holds more juice than a short wide glass with the same amount. This shows a lack of:
questions.explain: Failing conservation is typical of the preoperational stage.

questions.q: Ainsworth's Strange Situation was designed to assess:
options: The type or quality of infant attachment
questions.explain: It classifies attachment as secure, insecure-avoidant or insecure-resistant.

questions.q: Bowlby proposed that early attachment provides:
options: An internal working model shaping later relationships
questions.explain: The internal working model is a template from early attachment influencing later relationships.

questions.q: Enculturation is the process of:
options: Learning the norms and values of one's own culture
questions.explain: Enculturation is acquiring one's own culture's norms; adapting to a new culture is acculturation.

questions.q: Rutter's studies of Romanian orphans are used to show the effects of:
options: Early deprivation on development, moderated by later care
questions.explain: Early institutional deprivation affected development, with recovery influenced by the timing of adoption and later care.

questions.q: Which attachment classification is NOT one of Ainsworth's three?
questions.explain: Ainsworth identified secure, insecure-avoidant and insecure-resistant attachment.

questions.q: Peers become an increasingly important influence on identity during:
questions.explain: Peer influence on behaviour and identity grows through childhood and adolescence.

questions.q: A migrant child keeps their heritage language at home while adopting the host culture at school. This blending reflects:
questions.explain: Adapting to a new culture while maintaining heritage culture is acculturation (integration).

questions.q: A methodological point about classic attachment research is that:
options: Attachment norms can vary across cultures, so caution is needed generalising
questions.explain: Cross-cultural variation in caregiving means attachment classifications may not transfer unchanged (avoid imposed etic).

questions.q: A study that follows the same children over many years uses which design?
questions.explain: Longitudinal designs track the same individuals over time, strong for studying change but prone to attrition.

questions.q: Development is best explained as the result of:
questions.explain: Development reflects maturation plus experience and culture — nature and nurture together.
